clinicalPearls: An autosomal dominant autoinflammatory disease caused by heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in TNFAIP3, which encodes the NF-kappaB regulator A20.
Presents as early-onset Behcet-like disease with recurrent oral and genital ulceration, often from infancy or early childhood.
Recurrent fevers, arthralgia or arthritis, gastrointestinal inflammation (including an inflammatory bowel disease-like enterocolitis) and skin lesions are common.
Autoimmune features and autoantibodies frequently coexist, overlapping with lupus, autoimmune thyroid disease and other autoimmunity, making it broader than classic Behcet disease.
A strong autosomal dominant family history with variable expressivity is typical, and the pathergy test is often negative unlike sporadic Behcet disease.
A20 restrains both NF-kappaB signalling and the NLRP3 inflammasome, so haploinsufficiency drives excess interleukin-1, interleukin-6 and tumour necrosis factor.
Treatment is directed at the dominant cytokines, with colchicine, tumour necrosis factor inhibitors and interleukin-1 blockade all used.
reference.pathophysiology: A20, encoded by TNFAIP3, is a dual-function ubiquitin-editing enzyme with an amino-terminal deubiquitinase (OTU) domain and carboxy-terminal zinc-finger domains that carry E3 ligase and ubiquitin-binding activity; it terminates NF-kappaB signalling downstream of tumour necrosis factor, Toll-like and NOD-like receptors and also restrains the NLRP3 inflammasome. Heterozygous germline loss-of-function or truncating mutations reduce functional A20 below the threshold needed to control these pathways (haploinsufficiency), leading to sustained NF-kappaB activation, enhanced inflammasome activity and overproduction of pro-inflammatory cytokines including tumour necrosis factor, interleukin-1 and interleukin-6. The resulting systemic autoinflammation manifests as an early-onset Behcet-like syndrome, and the loss of immune regulation also predisposes to autoantibody formation and overt autoimmunity.
additionalDifferentials: Systemic lupus erythematosus and other systemic autoimmune diseases
Inflammatory bowel disease, including very-early-onset disease
Hereditary periodic fever syndromes (familial Mediterranean fever, TNF receptor-associated periodic syndrome, mevalonate kinase deficiency)
Other monogenic NF-kappaB-opathies such as relopathies and OTULIN deficiency
additionalInvestigations: Sequencing of TNFAIP3, ideally within a monogenic autoinflammatory and inflammatory bowel disease gene panel
Acute-phase reactants measured during and between flares
Autoantibody screen including antinuclear antibodies, anti-double-stranded DNA and thyroid antibodies
Functional studies of NF-kappaB activation and pro-inflammatory cytokine profiling
Ileocolonoscopy with biopsy when gastrointestinal disease is present
HLA-B51 typing, usually negative and helpful in distinguishing from classic Behcet disease
redFlags: Recurrent oral and genital ulceration beginning in infancy or early childhood
Central nervous system involvement or thrombosis in a Behcet-like pattern
Features of macrophage activation or overwhelming systemic inflammation
Strong multigenerational family history of Behcet-like disease
reference.prognosis: The course is chronic and relapsing with variable severity even within the same family; many patients do well on anti-inflammatory or cytokine-targeted therapy, though refractory gastrointestinal, ocular or neurological disease can cause significant morbidity.
pitfalls: Diagnosing sporadic Behcet disease and missing the monogenic, heritable cause in a child with a positive family history.
Expecting HLA-B51 positivity or a positive pathergy test, which are often absent.
Attributing the enterocolitis solely to classic inflammatory bowel disease.
Underestimating the overlapping autoimmune component and associated autoantibodies.
Overlooking at-risk relatives who warrant assessment given autosomal dominant inheritance.
references: International Union of Immunological Societies (IUIS) inborn errors of immunity classification
Textbook of autoinflammatory diseases and paediatric rheumatology references
management: Target the driving cytokines with biologic therapy, using tumour-necrosis-factor inhibitors, interleukin-1 blockade, or interleukin-6 receptor blockade according to the dominant manifestation
Use colchicine and glucocorticoids to control mucocutaneous ulceration and acute autoinflammatory flares
Add conventional immunosuppressants for autoimmune or organ involvement, with Janus kinase inhibition considered in refractory disease
Manage the inflammatory-bowel-disease-like enterocolitis jointly with gastroenterology
Monitor acute-phase reactants, disease activity, and autoantibodies, with regular ophthalmological review for uveitis
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across immunology, rheumatology, gastroenterology, and ophthalmology
Offer genetic counselling and family screening given autosomal dominant inheritance with variable expressivity
Consider haematopoietic stem cell transplantation for severe treatment-refractory disease
